research_question: Among adults undergoing cardiac surgery through a sternotomy, what is the effect of placing an implantable gentamicin-collagen sponge (gentamicin-impregnated collagen implant) locally in the sternal wound during closure, compared with no topical antimicrobial, on superficial surgical site infection?
treatment_label: Implantable gentamicin-collagen sponge placed locally in the sternotomy wound during closure
control_label: No topical antimicrobial in the sternotomy wound (usual care, including equivalent systemic antibiotic prophylaxis, permitted)
outcome_description: Single dichotomous target outcome: superficial surgical site infection of the sternotomy wound (event/no event), as defined by each trial. Extract the reported number of superficial SSI events and total randomized participants in each arm. Do not use deep SSI, mediastinitis, or combined/total SSI figures.
positive_direction: For standardized directional coding, a positive effect means the gentamicin-collagen sponge favors treatment by reducing superficial SSI versus no topical antimicrobial. For the requested Risk Ratio itself, RR < 1 favors the gentamicin-collagen sponge and RR > 1 favors control.
search_queries: gentamicin collagen sponge sternotomy superficial surgical site infection trial
gentamicin impregnated collagen implant cardiac surgery controlled comparison
local gentamicin collagen sternal wound superficial infection randomized trial
inclusion_criteria: Original empirical studies of adults undergoing cardiac surgery through a sternotomy that compare a locally implanted gentamicin-collagen sponge or gentamicin-impregnated collagen implant during wound closure with no topical antimicrobial/usual wound closure.

Studies reporting superficial sternotomy surgical site infection as a distinct dichotomous outcome, with quantitative arm-level information sufficient or potentially obtainable for effect-size calculation.

Any eligible cardiac surgical procedure, care setting, publication language, or publication status; concomitant systemic perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis is allowed when it does not constitute the topical comparison.
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study, including systematic reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, opinion pieces, protocols without results, and theoretical papers.

No comparison between the specified gentamicin-collagen implant treatment and a control condition receiving no topical antimicrobial; this excludes studies of only systemic antibiotics, antiseptic washes, other topical antimicrobials, or non-collagen gentamicin delivery.

No quantitative outcome data capable of producing the requested effect size (superficial SSI events and denominators, or recoverable equivalent data such as proportions); studies reporting only deep SSI, mediastinitis, or a combined/total SSI figure without separable superficial SSI data are excluded from this analysis.
Completely unrelated to the research topic, including studies outside adult cardiac sternotomy wound management or studies not evaluating the specified gentamicin-collagen sponge/implant.
moderators_to_extract: Gentamicin-collagen sponge dose, size, and number of implants
Trial definition and ascertainment method for superficial SSI
Baseline infection-risk profile, including diabetes, obesity, and reoperation/emergency status
effect_size_note: Pool superficial SSI as a Risk Ratio (RR) using each trial's reported superficial SSI event count and total randomized per arm, preferably by intention to treat. Keep deep SSI/mediastinitis and combined or total SSI out of this outcome. Use log RRs and inverse-variance weights for synthesis, report pooled RR with 95% CI, and state that RR < 1 favors the implant. Prespecify a random-effects model with a common-effect sensitivity analysis; estimate heterogeneity with tau-squared and I-squared. For a study with zero events in one arm, apply the prespecified continuity-correction method needed to estimate an RR; studies with zero superficial SSI events in both arms are non-informative for conventional RR pooling and should be described and addressed in sensitivity analysis. Avoid double-counting participants across multiple reports of the same trial.
